PSYCHIATRIC__Low Mood:
Low mood is a symptom, and the first move is always to assess risk.
  • Before anything else, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and means — a positive answer changes the plan immediately (see self-harm & suicidal ideation).
  • Then decide: is this clinical depression, and is it unipolar or bipolar? Core depression is persistent low mood, anhedonia and low energy for ≥2 weeks with cognitive and biological symptoms (see depressive disorders). Always ask about past mania / hypomania — bipolar depression must not be treated with antidepressant monotherapy (see bipolar disorder, mania).
  • And exclude organic causes: hypothyroidism, anaemia / B12 deficiency, drugs (steroids, beta-blockers, alcohol), Cushing’s, Parkinson’s, dementia and occult malignancy (see hypothyroidism, anaemia, substance use). Don’t forget bereavement and adjustment, and comorbid anxiety.
🚨Assess suicide risk in everyone with low mood. Ask about ideation, plans, intent, means, and protective factors; escalate for a specific plan, intent, access to means, previous attempts, or command hallucinations (see self-harm & suicidal ideation, self-harm & suicide risk). Severe / psychotic depression — delusions of guilt, poverty or nihilism (Cotard’s), catatonia, or severe self-neglect and dehydration — is a psychiatric emergency needing urgent assessment (± ECT) (see depressive disorders). Screen for bipolarity (a past “high”) before prescribing (see bipolar disorder), and think of postnatal depression (and puerperal psychosis) in the perinatal period.

  • A past episode of mania / hypomania (elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, overspending, grandiosity)

  • Needs a mood stabiliser-based plan
🟠Organic cause
  • Hypothyroidism, anaemia / B12 deficiency, Cushing’s, Parkinson’s, dementia, occult cancer (see hypothyroidism, anaemia)

  • Grief — proportionate to a loss, comes in waves, preserved self-worth
  • Adjustment disorder after a stressor; seasonal affective disorder
  • Comorbid anxiety is common (see anxiety)

PSYCHIATRIC__Anxiety:
Anxiety is excessive fear or worry with autonomic arousal — palpitations, sweating, tremor, chest tightness, breathlessness and a sense of dread.
  • The essential first step is to exclude the physical “masqueraders”, because several dangerous conditions present exactly like a panic attack: acute coronary syndrome, an arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, hypoglycaemia and thyroid storm (see acute coronary syndrome).
  • Then screen for endocrine and drug causes — hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, caffeine / stimulants and alcohol / benzodiazepine withdrawal (see hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, substance use).
  • Only then classify the primary anxiety disorder: generalised anxiety disorder (persistent free-floating worry), panic disorder (recurrent unexpected panic attacks), phobias (specific, social, agoraphobia) and health anxiety (see anxiety & stress-related disorders). Anxiety very commonly coexists with depression, PTSD and OCD (see low mood, PTSD, OCD).
🚨Do not label a first “panic attack” without excluding a physical emergency. Chest pain with cardiac risk factors needs an ECG and troponin to exclude acute coronary syndrome or an arrhythmia (see acute coronary syndrome); sudden breathlessness with risk factors needs a PE work-up; and always check a capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia). Endocrine mimics are treatable: hyperthyroidism (weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, tachycardia) and phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating) (see hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma). Consider substance / withdrawal states (see substance use), and screen for comorbid depression and suicide risk (see low mood).

PSYCHIATRIC__Psychosis:
Psychosis is a loss of contact with reality — hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder and loss of insight. The golden rule is that a first episode of psychosis is organic until proven otherwise.
  • Before reaching for a psychiatric label, exclude delirium (an acute, fluctuating, clouded consciousness with disorientation and, classically, visual hallucinations — find and treat the cause) (see delirium, confusion / delirium).
  • Exclude drugs and withdrawal (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, steroids; alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens) (see substance use), and medical / neurological causes (autoimmune encephalitis, temporal-lobe epilepsy, Lewy body dementia).
  • Only then classify the functional psychoses: schizophrenia (see schizophrenia / psychosis), mood psychoses (psychotic depression and mania) (see low mood, mania), schizoaffective and delusional disorder. Puerperal psychosis is a postpartum emergency (see postpartum complications).
🚨Screen every first-episode psychosis for an organic cause. Delirium (clouded / fluctuating consciousness) demands a search for infection, metabolic disturbance, drugs and CNS disease (see delirium). Autoimmune (anti-NMDA-receptor) encephalitis — psychosis with confusion, seizures, movement disorder and autonomic instability in a young person — is treatable and must not be missed (see encephalitis). Puerperal psychosis (rapid-onset postpartum psychosis / confusion) is a psychiatric emergency (see postpartum complications). Assess risk throughout — command hallucinations, delusion-driven acts, suicide and neglect — and remember drug-induced psychosis (stimulants, cannabis) (see substance use).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Delirium (organic psychosis)
  • Acute onset, fluctuating course, clouded consciousness, disorientation, inattention
  • Classically visual hallucinations → find and treat the cause (infection, metabolic, drugs, CNS) (see delirium, confusion / delirium)
  • Not schizophrenia — the level of consciousness is impaired
🚩Encephalitis / CNS cause
  • Autoimmune (anti-NMDA) or infective encephalitis — psychosis + confusion, seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability
  • Temporal-lobe epilepsy, tumour, Lewy body dementia (see encephalitis)
  • LP + MRI + antibodies; treatable
🚩Puerperal psychosis / risk
  • Rapid-onset postpartum psychosis / confusion — a psychiatric emergency (see postpartum complications)
  • Command hallucinations, delusion-driven acts, suicide / harm to others or infant
  • Assess and manage risk urgently
🟠Drug-induced / withdrawal
  • Stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, steroids; alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens (see substance use)
  • Onset relates to use / cessation; often resolves
  • Urine drug screen; treat withdrawal
🟠Schizophrenia / functional
  • ≥1 month of delusions, auditory hallucinations (third-person / running commentary), thought disorder, passivity
  • Negative symptoms (blunted affect, avolition, social withdrawal), preserved consciousness (see schizophrenia / psychosis)
  • Schizoaffective / delusional disorder are relatives
🩹Mood psychosis
  • Psychotic depression — nihilistic / guilt delusions (see low mood)
  • Mania with grandiose delusions and pressured speech (see mania)
  • Mood-congruent psychosis; treat the mood disorder
Consciousness is the great divider. Clouded / fluctuating consciousness = delirium (organic — find the cause). Clear consciousness with delusions / hallucinations for ≥1 month points to a functional psychosis — but still screen for drugs and encephalitis.

PSYCHIATRIC__Mania:
Mania is elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and activity.
  • The symptom cluster is DIGFAST — Distractibility, Insomnia (reduced need for sleep), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, increased Activity, pressured Speech and Thoughtless risk-taking (spending, sex, driving).
  • Mania lasts ≥1 week with marked impairment (± psychosis); hypomania lasts ≥4 days without severe impairment or psychosis (see bipolar disorder).
  • As with any first presentation, exclude secondary causes: drugs (steroids, dopamine agonists, stimulants, an antidepressant-induced switch) (see drug reactions, substance use), hyperthyroidism (see hyperthyroidism), and frontal-lobe pathology or delirium.
  • Assess risk throughout — financial, sexual, physical exhaustion, and psychosis (see psychosis, self-harm & suicidal ideation).
🚨Acute mania is a psychiatric emergency of risk. Manic patients can bankrupt themselves, drive dangerously, become sexually disinhibited, and reach physical exhaustion and dehydration; grandiose or persecutory psychosis may drive dangerous acts (see psychosis). Screen for secondary mania — corticosteroids, dopamine agonists, stimulants and an antidepressant-induced switch (see drug reactions), and hyperthyroidism (see hyperthyroidism). Do not forget that mania is one pole of bipolar disorder — an antidepressant given for the depressive phase can trigger a switch, and lithium / valproate have their own toxicity and (valproate) teratogenicity (see bipolar disorder).

PSYCHIATRIC__Memory Loss:
The first question in memory loss is: acute or chronic?
  • Acute memory impairment is usually delirium (an organic, fluctuating, inattentive confusional state — find the cause) (see delirium, confusion / delirium), or a discrete event — Wernicke’s encephalopathy, transient global amnesia, head injury or seizure (see Wernicke-Korsakoff, transient global amnesia).
  • Chronic, progressive memory loss suggests dementia (Alzheimer’s, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal) (see dementias).
  • The crucial task is to catch the reversible “dementia mimics”: depression (pseudodementia) (see depressive disorders, low mood), hypothyroidism, B12 / folate deficiency (see hypothyroidism, anaemia), normal-pressure hydrocephalus (dementia + gait apraxia + incontinence) (see hydrocephalus), and medications / alcohol. Always take a collateral history.
🚨Some memory loss is a treatable emergency. Wernicke’s encephalopathy — the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus and ataxia, classically in an alcohol-dependent or malnourished patient — needs immediate parenteral thiamine to prevent irreversible Korsakoff’s amnesia (give thiamine before or with glucose — but never withhold glucose from a hypoglycaemic patient) (see Wernicke-Korsakoff). Acute memory loss is often delirium — screen for infection, drugs and metabolic causes (see delirium). Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (the triad of dementia, a magnetic gait and urinary incontinence) is reversible with shunting (see hydrocephalus). And depression can masquerade as dementia (pseudodementia) — and is treatable (see depressive disorders).

PSYCHIATRIC__Sleep Disturbance:
Sleep disturbance is a symptom to explain, not a diagnosis. Sort it into insomnia (difficulty falling / staying asleep), hypersomnia (excessive daytime sleepiness), circadian problems (shift work, jet lag, delayed sleep phase) and parasomnias (sleepwalking, terrors, REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmares).
  • Most insomnia is secondary — to depression (early-morning waking), anxiety (a racing mind at sleep onset), pain, caffeine, alcohol and drugs (see low mood, anxiety).
  • The most important medical cause of unrefreshing sleep is obstructive sleep apnoea — loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime somnolence, with real cardiovascular risk (see obstructive sleep apnoea, snoring & apnoeas).
  • Don’t miss the psychiatric flags: a reduced need for sleep in mania and insomnia with suicidal depression (see mania). Consider restless legs, narcolepsy and REM sleep behaviour disorder (see restless legs, sleep disorders).
🚨Sleep symptoms can flag serious disease. Obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring + witnessed apnoeas + daytime somnolence, often with obesity and hypertension) raises the risk of road-traffic accidents, hypertension, arrhythmia and stroke — it needs a sleep study and CPAP (see obstructive sleep apnoea). A markedly reduced need for sleep with elevated mood is mania (see mania); insomnia with pervasive low mood should prompt a suicide-risk assessment (see low mood). REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams, punching / shouting) can herald Parkinson’s disease / Lewy body dementia years ahead (see Parkinson’s disease). And avoid the trap of long-term hypnotics / benzodiazepines.

PSYCHIATRIC__Eating & Appetite Changes:
Read eating and appetite changes on two axes: weight direction and appetite direction.
  • Weight loss with a poor appetite raises depression, malignancy and chronic disease; weight loss with a preserved / increased appetite points to hyperthyroidism or new type 1 diabetes (see hyperthyroidism, type 1 diabetes).
  • Weight gain follows hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, PCOS and drugs (antipsychotics, steroids) or atypical depression (see hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, PCOS, weight gain).
  • Then screen for the eating disorders: anorexia nervosa (restriction, low BMI, intense fear of weight gain), bulimia (binge–purge, usually normal weight), binge-eating disorder and ARFID (see eating disorders). Ask the SCOFF questions.
  • Two things are medical emergencies: the medically unstable anorexic (bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance, refeeding risk) and purging hypokalaemia (arrhythmia).
🚨The starved and the purging body can arrest. In anorexia nervosa, watch for medical instability — a very low BMI, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, prolonged QTc and electrolyte disturbance — and for refeeding syndrome (falling phosphate / potassium / magnesium on feeding) which can be fatal (see eating disorders). Purging in bulimia causes hypokalaemia and arrhythmia, a metabolic alkalosis and Russell’s sign (knuckle callus). Do not miss organic weight loss: malignancy (unintentional loss + red flags), hyperthyroidism, and new type 1 diabetes presenting with weight loss, polyuria and thirst — which can proceed to DKA (see hyperthyroidism, type 1 diabetes).

PSYCHIATRIC__Self-Harm & Suicidal Ideati:
Self-harm and suicidal ideation need two things at once: treat the body, and assess the risk.
  • First, manage the act medically — resuscitate, treat the overdose (a paracetamol level and N-acetylcysteine, ECG for a tricyclic, naloxone for an opioid), and manage a ligature injury or bleeding (see drug overdose & toxicology).
  • Then perform a structured psychosocial risk assessment: the current ideation, plan, intent, access to means and preparatory acts, previous attempts, and the protective factors (see self-harm & suicide risk).
  • Look for the underlying psychiatric illness — depression, psychosis, bipolar disorder, personality disorder and substance misuse (see low mood, psychosis, substance misuse).
  • Distinguish self-harm as emotional regulation (often without suicidal intent) from a suicide attempt, and address capacity if the patient refuses care (see personality disorders, mental health law & capacity).
🚨Never leave a patient at active risk unassessed or alone. High-risk features include a clear plan, ongoing intent, a high-lethality method, access to means, preparatory acts (a note, giving away possessions), previous attempts, and command hallucinations (see psychosis). Static risk factors: older age, male sex, social isolation, chronic illness / pain, substance misuse, recent loss and psychiatric illness (see self-harm & suicide risk). Treat every overdose seriously — a staggered or unknown paracetamol overdose, a tricyclic (arrhythmia, seizures) or opioid ingestion can kill (see drug overdose & toxicology). If a patient refuses treatment, assess capacity and consider the Mental Health / Capacity Act (see mental health law & capacity).

PSYCHIATRIC__Agitation / Aggression:
Acute agitation or aggression is a symptom to be made safe and then explained.
  • The reflex is to exclude an organic cause first — delirium (acute, fluctuating, inattentive), hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention or constipation, pain, head injury and drug intoxication / withdrawal (see delirium, confusion / delirium).
  • Alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens) and stimulant intoxication are common, dangerous causes (see substance use, substance misuse).
  • Then consider the psychiatric causes: psychosis and mania (see psychosis, mania), the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) (see dementias), and situational distress or a personality disorder (see personality disorders).
  • Management runs in order: ensure safety → de-escalate → treat the cause, with rapid tranquillisation only when de-escalation fails (see psychotropic drug classes).
🚨Assume agitation is organic until proven otherwise — and keep everyone safe. Always check a capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia), oxygen saturation (hypoxia), and screen for sepsis, retention, pain and head injury (see delirium). Alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens (tremor, sweating, hallucinations, seizures) needs prompt benzodiazepines and thiamine (see substance use). Beware neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome (rigidity / clonus + hyperthermia + autonomic instability) in an agitated patient on psychotropics. Use the least-restrictive approach — environment and de-escalation first — and reserve rapid tranquillisation for imminent risk, with monitoring (see psychotropic drug classes).

PSYCHIATRIC__Medically Unexplained Sympt:
Medically unexplained symptoms are physical symptoms without an adequate organic explanation after appropriate assessment.
  • Two principles guide the whole approach: take the symptoms seriously (they are real and distressing, not “made up”), and investigate proportionately — enough to exclude organic disease, but not so much that over-investigation reinforces illness behaviour.
  • The spectrum runs from somatic symptom disorder (distressing somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts, feelings and behaviours) and illness anxiety disorder (health anxiety) to conversion (functional neurological) disorder (neurological symptoms inconsistent with disease, e.g. a positive Hoover’s sign) (see somatisation / MUS, Hoover’s sign).
  • Crucially, depression and anxiety commonly present with physical symptoms (see low mood, anxiety). At the far end sit factitious disorder (intentional feigning for the sick role) and malingering (feigning for external gain).
🚨“Medically unexplained” is a diagnosis of appropriate exclusion, not of dismissal. Serious organic disease can present with vague or fluctuating symptoms — early multiple sclerosis, SLE, phaeochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism, coeliac disease and occult malignancy — so new red-flag symptoms (focal neurology, weight loss, night sweats, PR bleeding) always warrant targeted investigation. Equally, avoid the harm of over-investigation and iatrogenic reinforcement. Recognise treatable depression and anxiety presenting somatically (see low mood, anxiety), and support functional disorders positively using confirmatory signs (Hoover’s, tremor entrainment) rather than by exclusion alone (see Hoover’s sign, somatisation / MUS).

PSYCHIATRIC__Substance Misuse:
Substance misuse presents in four ways: intoxication, overdose, withdrawal and dependence — plus the complications.
  • Recognise the emergencies first: an opioid overdose (pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + reduced consciousness → naloxone) (see drug overdose & toxicology); alcohol withdrawal (tremor → seizures → delirium tremens) and Wernicke’s encephalopathy → thiamine (see substance use, Wernicke-Korsakoff, memory loss); and stimulant toxicity (agitation, hypertension, chest pain, hyperthermia).
  • The dependence syndrome is defined by tolerance, withdrawal, a compulsion to use, difficulty controlling use, prioritisation over other interests, and persistence despite harm (see substance use).
  • Screen with AUDIT / CAGE, and look for the complications — blood-borne viruses, liver disease, social and mental-health harm (see HIV, alcoholic liver disease, low mood). Manage with harm reduction and substitution / detox.
🚨Three substance emergencies to know. Opioid overdose — pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced consciousness — is reversed with naloxone (short-acting, so re-dose / infuse) (see drug overdose & toxicology). Alcohol withdrawal escalates from tremor and sweats to withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic storm) — treat with a benzodiazepine regimen and give parenteral thiamine before or with glucose (never withhold glucose from a hypoglycaemic patient) to prevent Wernicke’s / Korsakoff’s (see Wernicke-Korsakoff). Stimulant toxicity can cause arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, hyperthermia and seizures. And screen every injecting user for blood-borne viruses and offer naloxone and vaccination (see HIV).

PSYCHIATRIC__Obsessions & Compulsions (O:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a cycle of obsessions and compulsions.
  • Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted, distressing thoughts, images or urges (contamination, doubt, symmetry, taboo / aggressive thoughts); compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts (washing, checking, ordering, counting) performed to neutralise the anxiety.
  • The hallmark is that they are ego-dystonic — recognised as excessive and resisted — and they consume time and impair function (see anxiety & stress-related disorders).
  • Distinguish OCD from its look-alikes: generalised anxiety (real-life worries, not rituals) (see anxiety), obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (rigid perfectionism that is ego-syntonic and not distressing) (see personality disorders), and psychosis (loss of insight, thoughts felt as externally imposed) (see psychosis).
  • Screen for comorbid depression (see low mood), and related disorders — body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, trichotillomania and tics / Tourette’s (see movement disorders).
🚨OCD is disabling, and its main danger is comorbid depression. Severe OCD consumes hours a day and causes profound impairment; comorbid depression is common, so screen mood and assess suicide risk (see low mood). Do not mistake OCD for psychosis — in OCD, insight is usually preserved and the thoughts are recognised as the patient’s own; a genuine loss of insight, or thoughts experienced as externally imposed, points to a psychotic disorder (see psychosis). Harm / taboo obsessions (e.g. fear of harming a child) are distressing but carry a low actual risk — reassure and treat, while remaining alert. In children, consider PANDAS (an abrupt, post-streptococcal onset) and neurodevelopmental disorders.

PSYCHIATRIC__Trauma & Stress Reactions (:
Trauma & stress reactions are the normal and pathological responses to a threatening or catastrophic event.
  • A person who has faced actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence may present with four symptom clusters: re-experiencing (intrusive flashbacks, nightmares, reliving the event), avoidance (of reminders, people or places), hyperarousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, insomnia, irritability) and negative alterations in cognition and mood (guilt, shame, emotional numbing, detachment) — the picture of post-traumatic stress disorder.
  • The critical variable is timing: an acute stress reaction (ICD) begins within days and settles within about 4 weeks (DSM terms this acute stress disorder, 3 days–1 month); an adjustment disorder is a sub-threshold reaction to an identifiable stressor (see anxiety & stress-related disorders); PTSD requires symptoms persisting beyond 1 month; and complex PTSD follows prolonged or repeated trauma.
  • Always screen for comorbid depression (see low mood) and substance misuse (see substance misuse), which drive the main danger — suicide and self-harm (see self-harm & suicidal ideation).
🚨The emergency in trauma reactions is active suicide and self-harm risk. PTSD carries a high burden of comorbid depression and substance misuse, and the combination markedly raises suicide risk — ask directly about suicidal ideation, plans and means (see self-harm & suicidal ideation). Do not miss an organic contributor: a head injury / traumatic brain injury sustained in the same event can mimic or compound the picture, and acute intoxication or withdrawal can masquerade as hyperarousal. Distinguish a dissociative flashback (a vivid reliving with preserved underlying insight) from true psychosis (see psychosis). Avoid benzodiazepines and single-session psychological debriefing — both are ineffective or harmful after trauma.

PSYCHIATRIC__Extrapyramidal Side-Effects:
Extrapyramidal side-effects (EPSEs) are movement disorders caused by dopamine (D2) receptor blockade.
  • They are the signature adverse effect of antipsychotics — especially the typical / first-generation agents (haloperidol) (see psychotropic drug classes) — but also of the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, which block D2 too (see adverse drug reactions).
  • There are four classic EPSEs, best remembered by their timing: acute dystonia (hours to days — sustained spasm, oculogyric crisis, torticollis), akathisia (days to weeks — an unbearable inner restlessness), drug-induced parkinsonism (weeks to months — bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor) (see movement disorders) and tardive dyskinesia (months to years — involuntary orofacial movements, often irreversible).
  • The two red-flag reactions are laryngeal dystonia (an airway emergency) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (see neuroleptic malignant syndrome), and the key mimic to exclude is serotonin syndrome.
🚨Two EPSE emergencies must never be missed. Acute laryngeal dystonia — spasm of the laryngeal / pharyngeal muscles — threatens the airway and is treated immediately with IM / IV procyclidine (an anticholinergic). Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a fluctuating consciousness, with a markedly raised creatine kinase — stop the antipsychotic, give aggressive supportive care and consider dantrolene / bromocriptine (see neuroleptic malignant syndrome). Distinguish NMS from serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, hyperreflexia and clonus, usually lower-limb predominant, after serotonergic drugs) — NMS is slower, with rigidity and hyporeflexia. Report the reaction via the Yellow Card scheme (see adverse drug reactions).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Acute dystonia (laryngeal = airway emergency)
  • Sustained muscle spasm within hours to days: oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus
  • Laryngeal / pharyngeal dystonia can obstruct the airway — a true emergency
  • Treat immediately with IM / IV procyclidine (anticholinergic)
🚩Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
  • Hyperthermia + lead-pipe rigidity + autonomic instability + altered consciousness, with raised CK
  • Stop the antipsychotic; aggressive supportive care; consider dantrolene / bromocriptine (see neuroleptic malignant syndrome)
  • Days-to-weeks onset with hyporeflexia — distinguish from serotonin syndrome
🟠Akathisia
  • An unbearable inner restlessness and inability to sit still, over days to weeks
  • Easily mistaken for worsening agitation / psychosis — a dangerous error (linked to suicide)
  • Reduce the dose or switch; propranolol (or a benzodiazepine short-term)
🟠Drug-induced parkinsonism
  • Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity and tremor over weeks to months, typically symmetrical (see movement disorders)
  • A symmetrical resting / postural tremor is common (see tremor)
  • Reduce dose / switch to an atypical; an anticholinergic (procyclidine) may help
🩹Tardive dyskinesia
  • Late (months to years): involuntary orofacial movements — lip-smacking, chewing, choreoathetosis (see movement disorders)
  • Often irreversible — anticholinergics worsen it
  • Stop / switch (to clozapine); consider tetrabenazine / valbenazine
🩹Serotonin syndrome (the mimic)
  • Rapid onset after serotonergic drugs: agitation, hyperreflexia and clonus (lower-limb predominant), hyperthermia
  • Contrast with NMS: clonus / hyperreflexia vs rigidity / hyporeflexia
  • Stop the serotonergic drug; supportive care ± cyproheptadine (see adverse drug reactions)
Timing tells you which EPSE. Hours → dystonia; days → akathisia; weeks → parkinsonism; months to years → tardive dyskinesia. Two are emergencies (laryngeal dystonia, NMS). Always ask about antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), not just antipsychotics.
